newsitem.title: USA: Clinton delights in poverty drop, income rise.
newsitem.headline: Clinton delights in poverty drop, income rise.

text.p: The Census Bureau reported Thursday that 1.6 million Americans climbed out of poverty last year and that household income was rising, news that had President Clinton and his re-election campaign crowing.

The Census Bureau said that in 1995, there were 36.4 million poor people living in the United States, 1.6 million fewer than recorded in 1994. It was the second straight year of decline in the poverty level.
The bureau also said that between 1994 and 1995, for the first time in six years, households in the United States experienced an annual increase in median income after adjusting for inflation.

The Census report said the average household's median income rose by $888 after inflation to $34,076 in 1995. However, it noted that household income has not recovered to its 1989 pre-recession peak of $35,421 in 1995 dollars.
Clinton ballyhooed the new statistics at every opportunity, talking about them at a Rose Garden bill-signing ceremony then again during a visit to Capitol Hill.
"It is clear that we are moving on the right track," Clinton said. "Today it is clear that more and more of our people are sharing in that prosperity."
Clinton said the drop in the poverty rate was the largest one-year decline in 27 years. Aides said he was referring to 1968, when the poverty level went down 2.3 million from 27.7 million in 1967.
The campaign of Republican candidate Bob Dole, who has accused Clinton of pursuing policies leading to shrinking paychecks, was not convinced.

"These cold economic statistics may please Bill Clinton, but they do nothing to comfort a homemaker trying to buy groceries or a wage earner worried about the next paycheck," said Dole campaign spokesman Nelson Warfield.
Charging that "economic anxiety is real in America today," Warfield said the Census data shows that median household income is still below the level it reached in 1989.
He said earnings of full-time workers, men and women, declined so that the improvement in household income is due primarily to more members of a household working.

The Census Bureau, a part of the Commerce Department, said its annual study of incomes found that incomes of white and black households rose, although Hispanic households suffered a drop and Asian and Pacific families saw no change.
The Centre on Budget and Policy Priorities, a Washington think tank, said in an analysis of the Census report that the improvements in poverty and income in 1995 were substantial.
But it said that while income grew for lower- and middle-income households, only the wealthiest fifth of the U.S. population has seen its average income return to pre-recession levels.
"The average income of each of the bottom four-fifths of the population remains below 1989 levels," the analysis said.
